body.text: Dhiraj Kumar was in North Campus on September 6 when a friend forwarded him news of a building collapse in South Campus. He assumed it was another routine collapse in Delhi, until he realised the building was a paying guest (PG) accommodation and began searching online to identify which one.
The building was in Satya Niketan. Dhiraj’s friend Pawan Kumar, 17, lived there.

Pawan, a first-year student from Auraiya in Uttar Pradesh, had finished class XII and reached Delhi on August 17 after securing admission to Motilal Nehru College. His family was overjoyed; he had come to the city with plans. Dhiraj had helped him find the PG.

Dhiraj called Pawan and reached the site around 4 pm. “We kept looking for Pawan and showed his photograph to the police, telling them he was my brother. I was not allowed to go inside,” he said. He later learned that some of the injured had been taken to the AIIMS Trauma Centre and went there. At around 10 pm, he learned Pawan was among the seven people killed in the collapse, which also injured others.

“I had got him that PG. I felt responsible and did not dare tell his father,” Dhiraj said. He initially told Pawan’s family the teenager was unwell and asked them to come to Delhi, breaking the actual news only the next morning. He said ambulances arrived late at the site and hospital staff blocked families from finding out what was happening; an officer, he alleged, misbehaved with them.

“This is not just about Pawan. This is not a new problem. In 2022 also, a building collapsed in Satya Niketan, and two labourers died,” Dhiraj said. Most PG buildings around Delhi University have cheap infrastructure, he said, and in many cases the owners do not live there. He and other students are demanding compensation for the affected families and regulation of PGs. “Our main demand is that someone must be held accountable. If this can happen to one child, it can happen to another.”

Five of the seven dead were students. The collapse has focussed attention on the relationship between Delhi’s planning framework and construction on the ground, and raised questions about how buildings used for student accommodation are regulated and inspected.

The 1962 Master Plan for Delhi was an attempt to bring order to the city’s rapid post-Independence transformation: overcrowding in the Old City, housing shortages, incompatible land uses, poor sanitation, industrial growth and a large influx of new residents. Its approach included zoning, neighbourhood units, decentralisation, large-scale public land acquisition and satellite “ring towns”, said Pilar Maria Guerrieri, a historian of architecture and urban planning.
As Delhi moves ahead with the Master Plan for Delhi 2047, questions remain about how the plan will address the relationship between planning, regulation and implementation on the ground.
Recurring failures

Each of Delhi’s master plans reflects a different approach to managing the city. The 1962 Plan sought to direct growth through land acquisition, separation of land uses, redistribution of population densities and the diversion of growth to regional centres. It targeted roughly five million residents by 1981; Delhi reached 6.22 million. Planners also underestimated how difficult it would be to control where and how that population would find land, housing and work, Guerrieri said.

“By 2001, that land-use logic remained, but the plan was already responding to a much larger metropolitan reality, with urban extension, environmental protection, heritage, multimodal transport, and decentralisation moving to the centre,” she said.

“By 2021, Delhi was explicitly understood as a complex metropolis that zoning alone could not manage,” she said. That plan addressed mixed use, transport, the environment, informal settlements, private-sector participation and coordination among multiple agencies across the wider National Capital Region—a shift, in her words, from controlling urban growth to managing metropolitan growth.

The Master Planwas more effective at defining what Delhi should look like than at delivering enough serviced land and affordable housing quickly enough, Guerrieri said. Population and economic growth outpaced land acquisition, infrastructure provision and formal construction. Even Delhi Development Authority (DDA) documents acknowledge the mismatch between projected and actual population, and the shortfall in housing for lower-income groups.

Delhi is governed through multiple, overlapping authorities and tiers of government, she added. The gap between plan and city is not simply a matter of people violating the plan; it is also what happens when an ambitious spatial model meets rapid demographic and economic change without the institutional capacity to keep pace.

On unauthorised colonies and informal settlements, Guerrieri pointed to a mismatch between the planning model and the housing market available to most of Delhi’s population. “Unauthorised colonies typically emerged where formal planning failed to supply legal, affordable residential land at the scale or speed required,” she said. Many were built on agricultural or non-residentially zoned land and later became candidates for regularisation.

Their persistence reflects a recurring pattern, she said: planning fails to accommodate certain forms of urbanisation, informal development fills the unmet demand, the government eventually regularises or services it, and the Master Plan is revised to recognise development that has already taken place. “Informality, in other words, is not external to Delhi’s planning history—it is one of the mechanisms through which Delhi has actually urbanised,” she said.

A Master Plan is prospective and normative, Guerrieri said: it represents what planners intend to produce. Historical maps, by contrast, allow researchers to reconstruct the city that was actually built. Comparing maps across periods shows former villages absorbed into the metropolis, agricultural land disappearing, roads preceding planned development, settlements emerging outside designated residential areas, a changing relationship with the Yamuna, and the filling in of space between earlier urban centres. The maps show urbanisation as an ongoing process rather than a sequence of completed planning visions, she said.

“That’s why I wouldn’t read the 1962, 2001, and 2021 Master Plans as three increasingly accurate portraits of Delhi,” Guerrieri said. “Read alongside historical maps, they look instead like three successive attempts to reconcile an imagined, regulated city with a metropolitan territory that kept transforming faster and differently than anticipated.”
Student housing and the planning gap

“Delhi’s master plans have historically treated housing as a tenure category—ownership, EWS [economically weaker sections], or group housing—rather than a life-stage or occupational category. So students never got a distinct planning box the way industrial workers or slum dwellers eventually did,” said Rajwardhan Singh, a public policy analyst and adviser to the Dilli Dehat Project. Universities and coaching hubs grew organically in areas such as Mukherjee Nagar, Old Rajinder Nagar and the North Campus belt, he said, and the DDA responded to that growth after the fact, through zoning tolerance rather than proactive provisioning.

The draft Master Plan for Delhi 2041 did name student housing explicitly. It proposed affordable rental housing complexes, including hostels, student housing and worker housing, near mass transit and educational hubs, with incentives through floor area ratio (FAR) norms and Rental Management Agencies. Singh said this was more than earlier plans had offered. The 2041 draft was never finalised; it was superseded by the Master Plan for Delhi 2047, notified in August 2026.

“When housing is unsafe or overcrowded, the landlord is the visible violator but rarely the root cause, since landlords are responding to a supply vacuum that public agencies created and then ignored,” Singh said. The DDA, in his view, should bear responsibility for never operationalising the rental and student-housing provisions it drafted, while the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) is equally accountable for enforcing building bylaws. Basement conversions into coaching centres and hostels, sealed fire exits and illegal floor additions are violations MCD inspectors are meant to catch, he said.

Universities that draw large student populations without providing proportional on-campus or affiliated housing are, in Singh’s reading, pushing their housing responsibility onto an unregulated private market. Fire departments and the Delhi Fire Service share responsibility where no-objection certificates (NOCs) were issued or never checked against actual occupancy, he said.

“The deeper governance issue is that Delhi’s institutional architecture was never designed for a single accountable owner of student housing as a policy area,” Singh said. The responsibility falls between the DDA’s land-use mandate, the MCD’s building and fire-safety enforcement, the district administration’s law-and-order and licensing role, and the university’s own campus boundary—and each agency treats it as someone else’s jurisdiction. Fire-safety compliance suffers most from this fragmentation, he said, because NOC issuance, structural approval and occupancy monitoring sit with different departments that rarely share data or coordinate inspections.

“Until Delhi builds a convergence mechanism that makes one authority answerable for student-housing outcomes end to end, these incidents will keep recurring under different names and different addresses,” he said.
An old warning, unheeded

“Even in 1956, the problem of overcrowding in Delhi, causing a strain on civic amenities, was acutely recognised, and an interim plan for the city drawn up while the final Master Plan was being worked upon and tabled in 1962,” said Vandana Vasudevan, an urban development researcher and author of Urban Villager: Life in an Indian Satellite Town. The foreword to the interim plan, written by Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, India’s first Minister of Health in the Nehru Cabinet, recommended public participation by urging people to give their views on the plan, she said.

“It is as if time has stood still for urban planning in India since 1956, because the issues remain the same as what Rajkumari Amrit Kaur was worried about in the interim plan: long commutes, urban sprawl, too much traffic, and pressure on civic amenities due to migration adding to the population,” Vasudevan said. “It is oddly comforting to know these issues are not new to citizens, but it is also a damning comment on urban development in modern India.”

Master plans in post-Independence India gradually dropped such consultative practices, she said, and have become top-down exercises marked by corruption and vested interests. In Greater Noida, for instance, the Master Plan drawn up during the Mayawati government was redrawn repeatedly, with colours representing institutional, commercial and industrial areas changed depending on which lobby held sway, she said.

As developers grew more powerful, people were priced out of the property market and pushed to the periphery as cities expanded outward, absorbing former rural areas, Vasudevan said. This holds true across urban India, and as people moved to the outskirts, commute costs and travel time increased, various academic studies have shown.

“To avoid that, people who are short of both time and money, like students, settle for substandard accommodation just to be close to their educational institutes. Unscrupulous builders exploit their desperation and provide poorly constructed tenements. This leads to tragedies like the one we just saw,” she said. She noted that in cities such as Delhi, established colleges are concentrated inside the city, while those on the outskirts often do not match them in quality. Students consequently prefer to live close to the institutions they consider stronger.
When the law exists but isn’t enforced

“Delhi’s construction is governed by multiple land-owning and regulatory agencies—the MCD, the DDA, the L&DO [Land and Development Office], the Public Works Department (PWD), the Railways, and the DUSIB [Delhi Urban Shelter Improvement Board], among them. Each controls construction on land under its jurisdiction through its own statute: the MCD Act, the DDA Act, the Master Plan for Delhi, and the Unified Building Bye-Laws. Fire safety sits separately with Delhi Fire Services,” said Anupradha Singh, a lawyer practising in Delhi. The framework itself is fairly comprehensive, she said; the problem lies elsewhere.

“The law exists, but it largely fails at the level of implementation. This is mostly due to non-action by the officials who are responsible for curbing illegal construction in the first place,” she said. Inspections that should happen before a building goes up often do not take place, and enforcement follows only after something has gone wrong—as seen in the sealing order and staff suspensions that followed the Satya Niketan collapse, she said.

She alleged that officials responsible for enforcing these regulations often ignore them in exchange for money, allowing owners and builders to bypass sanctioned plans, safety norms and structural requirements. That collusion, she said, does more to enable unsafe construction than any gap in the law itself.

On the legal consequences of a building collapse, Singh said there are two tracks. Criminally, the owner, builder, contractor or architect can be prosecuted for offences such as causing death by negligence, or culpable homicide where knowledge of the risk is shown, under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. Officials found complicit can face action under the Prevention of Corruption Act. Through civil remedies, victims and families can claim damages and compensation, including under the victim compensation scheme.

For Delhi’s next master plan, the challenge is not simply to produce another blueprint but to regulate the city that already exists, and to enforce that regulation with stronger coordination and accountability. The Satya Niketan collapse suggests that unsafe construction is rarely the result of a single violation. It reflects housing pressure, weak enforcement, and the distance between how Delhi is planned and how it actually grows.
This reporter reached out to DDA officials for a response but did not receive one. The story will be updated as and when the response arrives.
Jagisha Arora is a Delhi-based journalist covering social, gender, cinema, and political issues.
